3.text: lived the last years of his life as a wandering hunter of wild reindeer.¹

4.text: On the contrary, another Reindeer Chukchee, Ñĭroˊn,² had a shamanistic

5.text: call during his search for the herd which had run away in a thick fog. The

6.text: search lasted for several months, during which time Ñĭroˊn suffered severe

7.text: hardships. He was without food for days, had no shelter in which to sleep,

8.text: was drenched with rain, and was even without any fire to dry his clothes.

9.text: In this plight he met several animals who acted like men, and played various

10.text: tricks on him. At last he met a Wolf who was eating from a carcass

11.text: of a newly killed reindeer. The Wolf took compassion on him, saying that

12.text: he knew well what hunger was. He bade him cut off the legs of the car-

13.text: cass, and feed on the sinew and the marrow, which the Chukchee, as said

14.text: before, eat raw. The carcass, on its part, begged Ñĭroˊn not to touch it,

15.text: promising to bring his herd as ransom. The Wolf sneered at the proposition,

16.text: saying that the Reindeer was too slow, since it had allowed itself to be

17.text: caught. Then Ñĭroˊn ate from the carcass. The Wolf then promised to

18.text: find the herd. After two weeks he again met Ñĭroˊn, and told him where

21.text: and sacrificed it to the Wolf. From that time on, Ñĭroˊn considered himself

22.text: as “one with spirits” (eñeˊñɪlɪn). His claim, however, was generally ridiculed

23.text: by his neighbors on account of his character. He was a spendthrift, much

24.text: given to card-playing, and cared little for his herd and home, and the

30.text: Still another acquaintance of mine, by the name of Kaˊtek, from the

31.text: village of Uñiˊsak at Indian Point, entered into relations with the “spirits”

32.text: when he was of mature age, during a terrible adventure he had while hunting

33.text: seal. While walking on the ice-floe, along a wide crack, he happened to

34.text: harpoon a seal, which came out of the water at some distance from the edge

35.text: of the ice. With the ice-pick on the butt of his harpoon, he broke off a

36.text: piece of ice large enough to support his body, and ventured on it out toward

37.text: the seal, using the shaft of his harpoon as a paddle. Maritime hunters,

38.text: lacking a canoe, often do the same. Meanwhile a strong gale came from

39.text: the land and carried away the outer part of the ice-floe. Kaˊtek, who had

40.text: already reached his seal, was carried away on his piece of ice. Seeing his
